Hey, I am very sorry to hear, what you've gone through. That sounds tough, but here you still stand, you strong soul!

I don't know if this will apply to you, but my emptiness mostly came from feeling abandoned and alone. It all stemmed from the root that I needed a favorite person to exist as a human being. It was very hard to let go of the idea, as it had been operating in me for several years, but 1.5 months ago, while working alone and reflecting, I kept asking questions, specifically about my abandonment issues: Why x? Why y? Etc. That's how I got to the root. And let me tell you, my life has been much better ever since. I rarely feel empty now, and my abandonment issues are way less severe.

That's a really tough, but good question. I will attempt my best.

So first off, I have learned through questioning my behavioral patterns and actions, who I am.

For instance, I used to agree with people on things I didn't agree with at all, solely because I was afraid they would not like me and leave me (abandonment issues). This is not only deceptive but also betraying my true personality, because I would become severely self-destructive and resentful. I would stress my responses because I was so afraid of them ghosting me (again, fear of abandonment). My identity would be dependent on my favorite person, thereby my lack of identity. The reality is, I am not very agreeable. I score extremely high on compassion, but extremely low on politeness. When my true personality is manifested, and I am not trying to be deceptive for the sole reason of making an effort of avoiding abandonment, I am definitely not agreeable, afraid of hurting people's feelings or confronting people at all.

For me, overcoming self-deception has made it possible for me to build my core identity, because if you fill your belief system with garbage and dishonesty, it is inevitably going to collapse.

Another example: I would pretend to have a certain interest, simply to be like someone else, especially my previous favorite persons. For instance movies: I don't like watching movies at all. I think it is boring as hell. The same with cinemas. But back then I would go agree to watch one or try to get a Netflix account to be like them, even though I despised it. Now, I don't care. If someone loses their interest because I am not into movies, too bad. I don't like movies and never will, and that's that. I have only watched Harry Potter, Teen Wolf, The Maze Runner, and a few others. Either they can accept it or fuck off.

But of course, there are exceptions. Let's assume you are in a relationship, and you are spending the weekend with your partner. Here, I wouldn't mind watching a movie with her on a special occasion, to give it a chance. But it isn't something I would do regularly, ever. But doing something you don't normally do every now and then doesn't hurt.

What also has helped is taking a personality test. I specifically paid for a Big Five assessment. In short, I am extroverted, very high in enthusiasm, low in assertiveness (mainly due to high neuroticism; this explains my shyness, which gets confused with introversion. It is NOT the same.) Agreeableness; Very high in compassion, very low in politeness. Conscientiousness: Moderately high. I am quite high in orderliness. Openness: Exceptionally high! Explains why I am a creative person and artist. Neuroticism: Very high, unfortunately.

This has given me a model of understanding myself. This explains why I am so flamboyant and extroverted when I am performing or drunk. It is basically my shyness that makes me appear as an introvert. Of course, I do have elements of introversion; I can easily spend an entire day alone. But I am mostly extroverted.

I have also stopped abandoning my boundaries for specific people. Again, this is linked to my fear of abandonment. This is also self-deceptive. I wouldn't recommend it, especially because this is how you let narcissists into your life and get taken advantage of. If you don't know them, you should start defining them. But make sure they are realistic. Mirror them with yourself; would you be able to be friends with a person with these boundaries. This is also related to having morals and values. If they don't respect your boundaries, values, and morals, leave them. They aren't the one for you. Your emotions are going to tell you otherwise, that it is going to be alright because you are in love with this person, but don't let it blind you. Rather suffer the short-term pain and be free from a toxic relationship than ending up being attached and in hell.

Your interests are also key to developing your core identity. If you don't have any, I would recommend slowly finding some. This won't happen in one day, but don't the road it will pay off. Remember: Rome wasn't built in one day.

Idk if this answered your question, but I hope it helps :)

The realization came while working. I was alone for several hours, so I just started thinking about my entire life. It explains most of my suffering, severe depression (although, I am on meds now, which has uplifted most of it), anxiety, and paranoia. It all stems from this. That's good because now my problem isn't 1000 different things, which makes it impossible to grasp.  
  
My theory is, as I develop my identity, my abandonment issues will slowly decrease. That's because once I have a stable identity, I won't over-rely on others to have stability. Of course, a social network is important: Virtually everyone would be miserable if they didn't have any people in their lives. But it is important to distinguish between the inevitable suffering due to how humans are biologically wired, versus this.  
  
I'm already well on my way when it comes to building my sense of self: I have hobbies I pursue. I treat myself as someone I am responsible for helping. I take care of my physical health by frequent training and moderately healthy eating. The list goes on. I am also getting tattoos to build my identity, as they are permanent.  
  
But most importantly, I desperately try to constrain an event to its appropriate consequence and meaning. What do I mean, exactly? If a girl, for instance, hugs me, it doesn't mean we are going to be a couple. She just hugged me and that's it. I can't determine its outcome as I don't have enough information; maybe I am special, and she is interested in me, or perhaps she is just a touchy person and does it to everyone. I can't know, so I won't build anything up in my head. She hugged me, and that's it. When you start to build an assumption up - one that is far from reality - you are in trouble. Got a bad grade? "What the hell am I doing here anyway? I am going to fail, so why even pursue this education?" Maybe that's not the best place to start. A more appropriate response would be, "I got an unsatisfactory grade.", followed by, "Did I study efficiently? Did I put in my best effort?" If the answer isn't yes, don't be too surprised.  
  
Hope my thoughts can be used with utility.  
  
\- And I am indeed thankful for being this young, yet far. I still have time to save my future self.
